## What the chronicles say [Record]
Contested. The story that [Vytautas](../characters/vytautas.qmd)'s two sons, held as hostages by the Order, were poisoned in 1392 rests on a weak base, mainly the 16th-century Prussian chronicler Simon Grunau. Wikipedia's article on the Ostrów Agreement records the rumour that his sons Iwan and Georg were poisoned and adds that no reliable sources confirm such sons existed. Some historians call it a rumour. His wife Ona was freed and sent to Lithuania in 1392 or before. The place is unknown (the graph says Königsberg; verify).

## What really happened [Saga]
Adopted as canon for Book II with the doubt voiced in-world (Q11): Ona half-believes it was fever. In spring 1392 Šešiapirštis goes into Prussia for the boys and finds them already dead of poison, herb-lore, mundane. He lays himself in the bog afterwards. A ragana offers to buy them back with an Order child's blood, and Vytautas refuses: the pagan option is worse. Ona gets out by her own wits. This is the price of the second defection, and it ends Form 4.

## Consequences
Caused by the turn that [Ostrów](ev_ostrow.qmd) rewards (the graph orders the edge Ostrów → poisoning, the reverse of the book). It is the worst price paid in Form 4 and deepens Ona's silence toward her husband.

## Dramatisation
Book II ch. 9 "Kraujo Puta" (Vytautas and Šešiapirštis; spring to summer 1392; the Neman and Prussia). Ona's grief is in ch. 10 and ch. 20.
